title: Where is it? Position words

summary.text: A book is on your left. You walk to the other side of the room, and the same book is on your right. Did the book move? You will hide a lemon, lay a banana leaf, count steps and play a shelf game to find out how we say where things are. You will learn top and bottom, above and below, inside and outside, near and far, left and right, in front, behind and between. You will also find out which of these words change when you move, and which stay the same.
summary.art: A girl standing on one side of a low stool that has a steel tumbler on it, a lemon under it and a book on the floor beside it, with her own footprints showing that she has walked round from the other side.

intro.hook: The cat is on the bottom shelf, on the left. Which shape is hiding the cat?
intro.text: The green triangle is hiding the cat. You needed two clues to find her. 'Bottom' told you which shelf. 'Left' told you which end. Words like these are called position words. They tell where a thing is. In this lesson you will use many of them, and test which ones change when you move.
intro.art: A two-shelf wooden rack with three coloured cut-out shapes leaning on each shelf, and the tip of a cat's tail showing from behind the green triangle at the bottom left.

chart.title: A shelf with a top and a bottom

outcomes: I can say where a thing is with top, bottom, on, under, above and below.
I can say if a thing is inside or outside, and if it is near or far.
I can show my left hand and my right hand, and say what is on my left and on my right.
I can say what is in front of, behind, next to and between other things.
I can put a thing in its place when I hear position words, and tell someone else where to put it.
I can say which position words change when I move, and which stay the same.

terms.meaning: The place where a thing is.
terms.example: The position of the tumbler is on the stool.
terms.art: A steel tumbler on a low stool with an arrow pointing to it.

terms.meaning: The top is the highest part of a thing. The bottom is the lowest part.
terms.example: The lid is at the top of the dabba. The last murukku is at the bottom.
terms.art: A tall steel dabba with its lid labelled top and its base labelled bottom.

terms.meaning: Above means higher than another thing. Below means lower than another thing.
terms.example: The fan is above the bed. The mat is below the bed.
terms.art: A ceiling fan over a cot, with a rolled mat under the cot.

terms.meaning: On means resting on top of a thing and touching it. Under means below a thing, covered by it.
terms.example: The plate is on the table. The dog sleeps under the table.
terms.art: A plate on a table and a dog asleep under the same table.

terms.meaning: Inside means within the edges or walls of a thing. Outside means not within them.
terms.example: The rice is inside the pot. The spoon lies outside the pot.
terms.art: A pot of rice seen from above with a spoon lying beside it.

terms.meaning: Near means a short way off. Far means a long way off.
terms.example: From your bed, the pillow is near and the bus stop is far.
terms.art: A child on a bed touching a pillow, with a bus stop seen small through the window.

terms.meaning: The two sides of your body. Most people eat with the right hand. The left is the other side.
terms.example: Tie a thread on your right wrist. The hand with no thread is your left hand.
terms.art: A child holding up two hands, with a red thread tied on the right wrist.

terms.meaning: In front of you is the side your face looks at. Behind you is the side your back is on.
terms.example: In the bus queue, Meena is in front of you. Your sister is behind you.
terms.art: Three children in a queue seen from the side, all facing a bus.

terms.meaning: In the middle, with one thing on each side.
terms.example: On the plate, the sambar is between the rice and the poriyal.
terms.art: A steel plate with rice on one side, a vegetable on the other and a cup of sambar in the middle.

terms.meaning: Beside a thing, with nothing in the way.
terms.example: Your left chappal is next to your right chappal.
terms.art: A pair of chappals side by side at a doorstep.

explanations.concept: A position word needs two things
explanations.context: This card says what every position word does. You used this in the game Find the Lemon.
explanations.definition: A position word tells where one thing is, compared with another thing.
explanations.description: Where is the lemon? 'Under' is not an answer, because under what? You must name a second thing: under the stool. Here is a worked example. Where is the square in the row? It is between the circle and the triangle. You named two other shapes to say it. Now say where the triangle is.
examples: The spoon is inside the tumbler.
The tumbler is on the stool.
The kolam is in front of the door.
explanations.art: A lemon under a stool, with a dotted line joining the lemon to the stool and the word 'under' on the line.
explanations.one_view: "A position word needs two things" is a plain meaning, a rule people agreed on, or a fact anyone can check, so only one honest view exists.

explanations.concept: Top, bottom, above, below, on, under
explanations.context: This card is about the words for higher and lower. The picture is a rack with three shelves.
explanations.definition: Top, above and on are for the higher place. Bottom, below and under are for the lower place.
explanations.description: Look at the three shelves. The circle is on the top shelf, the square is in the middle, and the triangle is at the bottom. So the circle is above the square, and the triangle is below the square. Here is a worked example. What is below the circle? The square and the triangle are both lower, so both are below the circle. 'On' and 'under' are for things that touch or are very close: a cup on a table, a cat under the cot.
examples: The clock is above the door.
Your feet are below your knees.
The last idli is at the bottom of the stack.
explanations.art: A three-shelf rack with a ball on the top shelf, a box on the middle shelf and a pair of chappals on the bottom shelf.
explanations.one_view: "Top, bottom, above, below, on, under" is a plain meaning, a rule people agreed on, or a fact anyone can check, so only one honest view exists.

explanations.context: This card is about inside and outside. To use these words you first need an edge, such as a wall, a lid or a line.
explanations.definition: A thing is inside when it is within an edge or a wall. It is outside when it is not.
explanations.description: A box has walls. A kolam has a border line. A ring of thread on the floor has an edge. Each of these has an inside and an outside. Here is a worked example. In the picture, two counters are inside the ring and three are outside. To check, ask: would the counter have to cross the edge to get out? If yes, the counter is inside.
examples: The seeds are inside the lemon. The peel is on the outside.
You are inside the house. The crow is outside.
One foot inside the ring and one foot outside: you are on the edge.
explanations.art: A ring of red thread on a floor with two beans inside the ring and three beans outside.
explanations.one_view: "Inside and outside" is a plain meaning, a rule people agreed on, or a fact anyone can check, so only one honest view exists.

explanations.context: This card is about near and far. You tested these words in the Step Count.
explanations.definition: Near means few steps away. Far means many steps away. You must say near to what.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. From the door, the mat is 2 steps away and the bed is 9 steps away. 2 is fewer than 9, so the mat is nearer the door. Now stand at the window, where the bed is only 1 step away. Now the bed is the near one. The bed did not move. You did. So always say where you are counting from.
examples: From your house, the shop is near and the sea is far.
For a child in Kanyakumari, the sea is near.
The Moon is far from us. The Sun is much farther.
explanations.art: A room seen from above with footsteps drawn from the door to a mat, two steps, and from the door to a bed, nine steps.

chart.title: Steps from the door. The mat is at 2.

explanations.one_view: "Near and far" is a plain meaning, a rule people agreed on, or a fact anyone can check, so only one honest view exists.

explanations.concept: Left and right go with you
explanations.context: This card is about left and right. You tested them in the Turn-Around Test and in Face to Face.
explanations.definition: Left and right are the two sides of your own body. When you turn, they turn with you.
explanations.description: Your right hand is always your right hand. But the things on your right change when you turn. Here is a worked example. You face a red circle and a blue square, and the circle is on your left. Your friend stands on the other side and faces you. For her, the circle is on the right. Both of you are correct. So when you say left or right, say whose: 'on my left' or 'on your left'.
examples: Two people facing each other shake right hands. The arms cross over.
'The third house on the left' depends on which end of the street you enter.
On a bus, your left stays your left wherever the bus turns.
explanations.art: Two girls facing each other across a mat with a red circle and a blue square between them, each pointing to her own left.

chart.title: Same two shapes, seen from two sides

explanations.one_view: "Left and right go with you" is a plain meaning, a rule people agreed on, or a fact anyone can check, so only one honest view exists.

explanations.concept: In front, behind, between, next to
explanations.context: This card is about the words for things in a line, such as a queue.
explanations.definition: In front is the way a person or a line is facing. Behind is the other way. Between is in the middle of two.
explanations.description: Look at the row. It is a queue, and everyone faces right. The red circle is first, so nobody is in front of her. The blue circle is behind her. The yellow circle is between the blue and the green. Here is a worked example. Who is next to the green circle? Only the yellow circle, because nobody stands on green's other side.
examples: In a queue for the bus, the person in front of you gets on before you.
Your nose is between your eyes.
A chair has a front of its own, the side you face when you sit. Behind the chair is the side of its back rest.
explanations.art: Four children in a queue at a bus stop seen from the side, all facing the bus on the right.
explanations.one_view: "In front, behind, between, next to" is a plain meaning, a rule people agreed on, or a fact anyone can check, so only one honest view exists.

explanations.concept: Which words change when you move?
explanations.context: This card says what you found in the Turn-Around Test, where you looked at a stool from two sides and from far away.
explanations.definition: Some position words are about two things only. Others are about the two things and you.
explanations.description: 'The tumbler is on the stool' is about the tumbler and the stool. You are not in the sentence. So you can walk anywhere and it stays true. 'The book is on my left' has you in it. When you walk to the other side, it stops being true. 'The stool is near me' has you in it too. Walk away, and near becomes far.
examples: On, under and inside stay true when you move.
Left and right swap when you go to the other side.
Near turns into far when you walk away.
explanations.art: A child looking at a stool from one side, and the same child drawn again on the other side, with the book now on her other hand.

cols: When I walk to the other side
chart.title: What the test showed

explanations.one_view: "Which words change when you move?" is a plain meaning, a rule people agreed on, or a fact anyone can check, so only one honest view exists.

explanations.concept: Down is toward the middle of the Earth
explanations.context: This card is about the words up and down, top and bottom. It asks what 'down' means on a round Earth.
explanations.definition: Down is the way things fall: toward the ground, and so toward the middle of the Earth.
explanations.description: Drop a lemon, and the lemon falls down. The Earth pulls everything toward its middle, and we call that way down. The Earth is a ball, and people live all round the ball. A child in Chennai and a child in Peru, nearly on the opposite side, both stand with feet toward the middle. So 'down' for one child points a different way from 'down' for the other. Nobody is upside down. Inside the space station, astronauts float, and they have to agree which wall to call the floor.
examples: The top of a coconut tree is the end farthest from the ground.
Water in a tumbler always settles at the bottom.
A root grows down, toward the middle of the Earth.

perspectives.explanation: Down is just where things fall.
Heavy things fall because they seek their natural place at the centre of the world.
Newton said the Earth pulls everything toward its centre. Einstein described gravity as the bending of space and time by mass.

explanations.art: A round Earth with four small children standing on it at different places, each with feet toward the centre and an arrow labelled 'down' pointing to the centre.

explanations.concept: Everyone does maths: the bee's dance and the root
explanations.context: This card is about other living beings who know where things are and can tell others.
explanations.definition: Many living beings sense positions. Honeybees also tell each other how far and which way.
explanations.description: A honeybee finds flowers and flies home. Inside the dark hive she dances for her sisters. She runs in a straight line and waggles her body. A longer waggle means the flowers are farther away. The way her run points tells the others which way to fly, compared with the Sun. Karl von Frisch worked this out and won a Nobel Prize in 1973. Plants sense positions too. A root senses which way is down and grows that way, even in the dark.
examples: A short waggle run: flowers near the hive. A long one: flowers far away.
A run that points straight up on the comb means: fly toward the Sun.
Lay a sprouting seed sideways. The tip of the root bends to grow down again.

perspectives.explanation: A honeybee's waggle dance tells her sisters the direction and the distance of food, using the Sun as a guide.
Said the bees follow the smell of the flowers and not the dance. Radar tracking in 2005 showed bees do fly where the dance points.

explanations.art: A honeybee on a honeycomb making a figure-of-eight dance with a wavy line through its middle, while other bees crowd round her.

explanations.concept: People agree on left and right, and some do without them
explanations.context: This card is about the choices people have made about left and right.
explanations.definition: Which side to keep to, and even whether to use the words left and right, are things people chose.
explanations.description: On Indian roads, vehicles keep to the left. In many other countries they keep to the right. Neither side is better. What matters is that everyone on the same road agrees. Words are chosen too. The Guugu Yimithirr people of Australia mostly say north, south, east and west where we would say left and right. A speaker may say, 'The cup is to the east of the plate.' That sentence stays true whichever way you face.
examples: India, Sri Lanka and Japan keep left. France and the United States keep right.
The narrow tip of a banana leaf is often placed on the eater's left. Families chose that.
'The pot is by the east wall' works for everyone in the room.

perspectives.who: People who use left and right
perspectives.explanation: Left and right are about your body. A thing is 'left of the tree' from where you stand.

perspectives.who: The Guugu Yimithirr people of Australia
perspectives.explanation: They give directions in north, south, east and west for everything, even small things, so they do not need left and right.

explanations.art: A road in an Indian town with an auto and a bus keeping to the left, and beside it a small picture of a road in another country with cars keeping to the right.

agreed.text: To say where a thing is, you have to name another thing.
agreed.evidence: Try it. Say where your nose is without naming anything else. You will say 'between my eyes' or 'above my mouth'. There is no other way.

agreed.text: When two people face each other, one person's left is the other person's right.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it. Tie a thread on both right wrists and stand face to face. The two threads are on opposite sides.

agreed.text: Down is toward the middle of the Earth, so it points a different way in different places.
agreed.evidence: People live all round the Earth and nobody falls off. In 1522 the ship Victoria came back to Spain after sailing right round the world.

agreed.text: Even a child of three or four can work out what another person can and cannot see.
agreed.evidence: In 1975 a scientist named Martin Hughes asked small children to hide a doll from two toy policemen. About nine in ten gave the correct answer.

challenging.claim: My right is the same side as your right, always.
challenging.who: Many children, and grown-ups in a hurry
challenging.context: This card is about a common mix-up with left and right when two people face each other.
challenging.for: It is true when two people stand side by side and face the same way. Then both right hands are on the same side.
challenging.against: When they face each other, the right hands are on opposite sides. The test Face to Face shows it with two threads.

challenging.claim: Children below seven can only think about what they themselves see.
challenging.who: Jean Piaget and Bärbel Inhelder, two Swiss scientists, in the 1940s and 1950s
challenging.context: This card is about an old test with a model of three mountains, and a newer test that disagreed with it.
challenging.for: They sat children in front of a model of three mountains, with a doll on another side. Asked what the doll could see, many young children picked their own view.
challenging.against: In 1975 Martin Hughes used a simpler game: hide a doll from toy policemen. Most three and four year olds could do it. The mountain test may have been too strange for them.

challenging.claim: All people think of the world as left and right.
challenging.who: Many people who speak languages that have these words
challenging.context: This card asks whether left and right are built into every person, or learned from our language.
challenging.for: Every human body has two sides, and most languages have words for them.
challenging.against: Guugu Yimithirr speakers in Australia mostly use north, south, east and west for where things are. Scientists still argue about how much this changes the way they think.

big_questions.q: You turn around, and the book goes from your left to your right. What really changed?
big_questions.hint: Did the book move? Did the room move? Did you?

big_questions.q: Can you say where something is without naming any other thing?
big_questions.hint: Try with your nose, the Moon, or the lemon under the stool.

big_questions.q: Which words work the same for everyone in the room, wherever they stand?
big_questions.hint: Think of on, under and inside. Think of left and near.

big_questions.q: Is there a top of the world? Who decided?
big_questions.hint: Globes and maps usually put north at the top. The Earth floats in space with no ground under it.

big_questions.q: An ant walks under the table top, upside down. For them, which way is up?
big_questions.hint: The ant's feet hold the table. The Earth still pulls the ant down.

big_questions.q: If you were the only thing there was, could you be anywhere?
big_questions.hint: Near what? Above what? On whose left?

story.title: The Third House on the Left
story.note: Nila, her father, her aunt and Tank Street are made up. Buses in Madurai really are sent by other roads on the days of the big temple chariot festival.
text: On Saturday morning Nila helped her father get ready. Appa could never do the button on his own right cuff.
"Give me your right hand," said Nila. She stood facing him. He held out his hand, and she reached for it with her left.
"That's funny," she said. "Your right hand is on my left side."
"Hurry up, kanna," said Appa. "We will miss the bus."

They were going to Madurai to see Meena Athai's new house for the first time. Athai had told them the way on the phone the night before. Appa had said it three times so that he would not forget. "Get down at the flower market. Walk into Tank Street. The third house on the left. Blue gate."
Nila said it too, in her head, all the way on the bus. Third house on the left. Blue gate.

But that day was the day of the temple chariot. The big road was closed, and the bus went round by small roads. It did not go to the flower market at all. It stopped beside the old temple tank, and the conductor called, "Last stop! Everybody down!"
Appa took out his phone to call Athai. The screen was black. He pressed the button. He pressed it again.
"No charge," he said. "Never mind. Look." He pointed to a board on the corner. It said TANK STREET. "We are here anyway. Come."
Tank Street was long and straight. At the far end Nila could see heaps of orange and white, and people carrying baskets. In between there were houses on both sides, each with a gate.
"Third house on the left," said Appa, and he counted. "One. Two. Three."
The third house on the left had a brown gate. A grandfather sat on the step, reading his newspaper.
"Is this Meenakshi's house?" asked Appa.
"No Meenakshi here," said the grandfather. "I have lived in this house for forty years."
Appa scratched his head. He counted again from the corner. One, two, three. It was still the brown gate.
"Maybe she said the fourth house," he said. The fourth house had a green gate, and a dog who did not want visitors. "Maybe there are two Tank Streets," said Appa. He looked hot and worried.
Nila was not counting houses. She was looking at the far end of the street, at the orange and white heaps. They were flowers. Marigolds and jasmine.
"Appa," she said. "Where is the flower market?"
"Down there, at the other end. Why?"

"Athai thought we would come in from the flower market. So she would walk up this street from that end. Like this." Nila turned around, so that her back was to the flowers. Now she was facing the way Athai would face.

"When I stand like Athai, my left hand is on that side." She pointed across the road. "But we came in from the tank. We are looking the other way. Athai's left is our right. Like your cuff this morning."
Appa looked at his right hand. He looked at the two sides of the street. He looked at Nila.
"And her third house is not our third house," said Nila. "She counts from the flower end. So we must count from there too."
They did not have to walk all the way to the market. Nila looked along the right side of the street to the last house before the flowers. She counted back toward herself. "One. Two. Three."
The third gate from the far end was blue.
They walked to it. Before Appa could knock, the door opened. Meena Athai stood there with flour on her hands.
"There you are! I rang and rang. Did you get lost? I told you, third on the left."
"It was the third on the left," said Nila. "Your left. Not ours."
Athai laughed. "Next time I will say: the blue gate, on the same side as the neem tree."
"That is better," said Nila. "The neem tree stays in one place."
story.epiphany: For the parent: 'left' is not a fact about the street. It belongs to the person who is walking, and to the way she is facing. Athai's direction had a hidden starting point, the flower market. When Nila and her father came in from the other end, left became right, and the third house had to be counted from the far end. Nila solves it by turning her body to face the way her aunt would face.
ask: Appa counted three houses on the left. Why was that the wrong house?
Why did Nila turn around in the middle of the street?
Athai said she would use the neem tree next time. Why is that a better clue than 'on the left'?
How would you tell a friend the way to your door, so that it works from both ends of your street?
