experiments.title: The Turn-Around Test: which words change when you move?
experiments.context: In this test you set five things around a stool and say six sentences about where they are. Then you walk to the other side, and then far away. Before each move you guess which sentences will stop being true. You will find out which position words depend on you.
experiments.question: If I move to a new spot, which sentences about position stay true, and which stop being true?
experiments.predict: Before each move, put a bean on every sentence that you think will stop being true. Why do you think those ones will change?
experiments.fair_test: Nobody touches the stool or the things around it. Only the child moves. We check all six sentences after each move, in the same order.

materials.item: a low stool or a small chair
a steel tumbler and a spoon
a lemon or a small ball
a book and a plate
a thread or a rubber band for the right wrist
paper, a pencil and 6 beans or buttons

experiments.safety: Keep beans, seeds and other small things away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Set five things around a stool. Say six sentences. Guess, then check them from the other side and from far away.

experiments.record: A grown-up writes the six sentences in a table. After each move, put a tick if the sentence is still true and a cross if it is not. At the end the child says what they found, and the grown-up writes it under the table.

rows: The tumbler is on the stool
The lemon is under the stool
The spoon is inside the tumbler
The book is on my left
The plate is on my right
example_chart.title: What a finished table can look like

setup.art: A low stool in the middle of a floor with a steel tumbler on it, a spoon standing in the tumbler, a lemon on the floor under it, a book on the floor to one side and a plate on the floor to the other side.
setup.caption: 1. Set the five things around the stool.

setup.art: A child standing one step from the stool and facing it, with a red thread on her right wrist, the book on her left and the plate on her right.
setup.caption: 2. Stand here. Say the six sentences.

setup.art: The same child now standing on the opposite side of the stool and facing it, so that the book is by her right hand and the plate by her left.
setup.caption: 3. Guess first. Then walk to the other side and check.

flow.do: 1. Put the stool in the middle of the room. 2. Put the tumbler on it and the spoon in the tumbler. 3. Put the lemon under the stool. 4. Your child stands one step away, facing the stool. 5. Tie the thread on their right wrist. 6. Put the book on the floor on their left and the plate on their right.
flow.say: Look at the stool. Tell me where each thing is. Where is the tumbler? Where is the lemon? Where is the book?
flow.kid: Stand one step from the stool. Say where each thing is.

ask.q: Where is the spoon?
good: In the tumbler.
Inside the tumbler.

ask.q: Which side is the book on?
good: My left.
The side with no thread.

flow.parent: Write the six sentences from the chart on paper as your child says them. If left and right are shaky, point to the thread: the thread hand is the right hand.

rows: The tumbler is ON the stool.
The lemon is UNDER the stool.
The spoon is INSIDE the tumbler.
The book is on my LEFT.
The plate is on my RIGHT.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Turn-Around Test. You set five things around a stool and say six sentences about where they are.

flow.do: 1. Read the six sentences aloud. 2. Say that your child will soon walk to the other side of the stool. 3. Ask them to put a bean on each sentence that will stop being true. 4. Ask why. Do not say if they are correct.
flow.say: Soon you will walk to the other side and look back at the stool. Which sentences will stop being true? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will walk to the other side. Which sentences will change? Put a bean on each.

ask.q: Why did you put a bean on that one?
good: Because I will see it from the back.
Because everything will be the other way.
The book will be on my other side.

flow.parent: Many six-year-olds put beans on 'on' or 'under' too, or on nothing at all. Accept every guess that comes with a reason.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the Turn-Around Test. Before you move, you guess which of the six sentences about the stool will stop being true.

flow.do: 1. Your child walks round to the other side of the stool and faces it. 2. Read each sentence. 3. Your child looks and says true or not true. 4. Write a tick or a cross for each.
flow.say: Now look. Is the tumbler still on the stool? Is the book still on your left? Check with your thread.
flow.kid: Walk to the other side. Face the stool. Check each sentence. True or not true?

ask.q: The book did not move. Why is it not on your left now?
good: Because I moved.
I am facing the other way.
My left is on that side now.

flow.parent: On, under and inside stay true. The book is now on the right and the plate on the left. The stool is still near.
flow.context: This is step 3 of the Turn-Around Test. You walk to the other side of the stool and check each of the six sentences.

flow.do: 1. Your child comes back to the first spot. 2. Say they will now walk ten big steps away and turn to face the stool. 3. They guess with beans again and say why. 4. They walk, turn and check each sentence. 5. Write ticks and crosses.
flow.say: Now you will walk ten big steps away. Which sentences will stop being true this time? Why?
flow.kid: Guess with beans again. Walk ten big steps away. Turn and check each sentence.

ask.q: Which sentence changed this time?
good: The stool is not near now.
It is far.
Only the near one.

flow.parent: In a small room, go as far as you can, even into the next room. This time only 'near' changes. Left and right stay as they were at the first spot.
flow.context: This is step 4 of the Turn-Around Test. You walk far away from the stool and check the six sentences again.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands at the first spot again. 2. Ask what will happen to 'on' and 'under' if they look at the stool upside down. 3. They bend over and look back between their legs.
flow.say: Bend over and look at the stool between your legs. Is the tumbler under the stool now? Why not?
flow.kid: Bend over. Look at the stool between your legs. Is the tumbler still on the stool?
flow.parent: The picture looks upside down, but the tumbler still rests on the stool. 'On' and 'under' go by which way things fall, not by which way your head is.
flow.context: This is step 5 of the Turn-Around Test. You look at the stool upside down to see if 'on' and 'under' change.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child to say which words stayed and which changed. 3. Ask why. 4. Write their words under the table.
flow.say: Look at the ticks and crosses. Which words stayed true every time? Which words changed? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at your table. Which words stayed true? Which words changed? Say why.

ask.q: What do you think now? What did you see? Why is it so?
good: On, under and inside did not change.
Left and right changed when I went to the other side.
Near changed when I went far.
Those ones are about me. When I move, they change.

flow.parent: A good answer in your child's own words: some words are about the things only, and some are about me too.

check.q: A cup is on a table, on your left. You walk to the other side of the table. What is true now?
options: The cup is under the table
The cup is on the table, on my right
The cup is on the table, on my left
check.why: The cup is still on the table, because you did not touch it. But you now face the other way, so the cup is on your right. Picking 'on my left' means left was treated as a part of the room.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Turn-Around Test. You say what you found: which position words changed when you moved, and which stayed.

activities.title: Find the Lemon: clues with position words
activities.context: In this game one person hides a lemon and gives clues made of position words. Nobody may point. It shows that a clue works only when it names a second thing.
activities.problem: Can you find a hidden lemon from words alone? Can you give clues so good that nobody needs you to point?

materials.item: a lemon, or any small toy
the things already in one room: a table, a cot, a shelf, vessels

schedule.what: Hide a lemon and find it from position-word clues. Then swap.

activities.record: After the game, the child draws one hiding place and a grown-up writes the clue under it.

setup.art: A child with hands over her eyes while a grown-up puts a lemon inside a steel vessel on the lowest shelf of a kitchen rack.
setup.caption: 1. One person hides the lemon. The other closes their eyes.

setup.art: The grown-up with hands behind her back, speaking, with a speech bubble showing a vessel and a shelf.
setup.caption: 2. Give clues with position words. No pointing.

setup.art: The child lifting the lemon out of the vessel on the bottom shelf.
setup.caption: 3. Find it. Then swap.

flow.do: 1. Your child closes their eyes. 2. Hide the lemon inside or under something. 3. Give two clues with position words. 4. Keep your hands behind your back.
flow.say: Open your eyes. The lemon is inside something. That thing is on the bottom shelf.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Then listen to the clues. Find the lemon.
flow.parent: Good first clues use two position words, such as 'inside the pot, under the table'. Choose a place that is safe to reach.
flow.context: This is the first step of Find the Lemon. A grown-up hides a lemon and gives you clues made of position words.

flow.do: 1. Swap. You close your eyes and your child hides the lemon. 2. Your child gives the clues. 3. If they point, put their hands behind their back and ask for words.
flow.say: Now you hide the lemon. Tell me where it is with words only. No pointing.
flow.kid: Now you hide the lemon. Give clues with words. Keep your hands behind you.

ask.q: You said 'there'. Where is there?
good: Under the cot.
Behind the door.
Next to the pot.

flow.parent: Children often say 'there' or 'that side'. Each time, ask 'Which thing is it near? Is it on, under or inside?'
flow.context: This is step 2 of Find the Lemon. Now you hide the lemon and give the clues, without pointing.

flow.do: 1. Hide the lemon once more. 2. Give a broken clue: say only 'It is under.' 3. Wait for your child to ask 'Under what?' 4. Then give the full clue.
flow.say: Here is my clue. The lemon is under. Can you find it now? What else do you need to know?
flow.kid: Listen to this clue: 'It is under.' Is that enough? What must you ask?

ask.q: What was missing from my clue?
good: Under what?
You did not say the thing.
The name of the other thing.

check.q: Which clue tells you where the lemon is?
options: It is under the blue stool.
check.why: 'Under the blue stool' names a second thing, so you know where to look. 'It is under' leaves out the second thing. 'There' only works if someone points.

flow.context: This is the last step of Find the Lemon. You find out why a clue such as 'It is under' is not enough.

activities.title: Face to Face: where did my right hand go?
activities.context: In this activity two people tie a thread on their right wrists. They stand side by side, and then face to face. It shows that your right and another person's right are on the same side only when you face the same way.
activities.problem: When my friend faces me, is her right hand on the same side as mine?

materials.item: a thread or a rubber band for each person's right wrist

schedule.what: Tie threads on right wrists. Compare hands side by side, then face to face.

activities.record: Draw two stick people facing each other. Colour both right hands red.

setup.art: A mother and a daughter standing side by side facing the same way, each holding up a right hand with a red thread on the wrist.
setup.caption: 1. Thread on each right wrist. Stand side by side.

setup.art: The same two now standing face to face, right hands raised, the two red threads on opposite sides of the picture.
setup.caption: 2. Guess first. Then face each other.

setup.art: The two shaking right hands, with their arms crossing the space between them.
setup.caption: 3. Shake right hands. See how the arms cross.

flow.do: 1. Tie a thread on your right wrist and one on your child's. 2. Stand side by side, facing the same wall. 3. Both raise the thread hand.
flow.say: This is our right hand. Raise it. Are our right hands on the same side?
flow.kid: Stand next to your grown-up. Raise your thread hand. Same side?
flow.parent: Side by side, both right hands are toward the same wall.

chart.title: Side by side. Red is the thread hand.

flow.context: This is the first step of Face to Face. You and a grown-up tie a thread on your right wrists and stand side by side.

flow.do: 1. Hands down. 2. Say that you will now turn to face each other. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason before anyone turns.
flow.say: Now we will face each other. Will our thread hands be on the same side? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Soon you will face each other. Will the thread hands be on the same side? Guess.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Yes, because right is right.
No, because you will turn round.
I am not sure.

flow.context: This is step 2 of Face to Face. Before you turn to face your grown-up, you guess where the two thread hands will be.

flow.do: 1. Turn to face each other. 2. Both raise the thread hand. 3. Let your child look. 4. Then both shake right hands.
flow.say: Raise your thread hand. Look at mine. Are they on the same side now? What happened?
flow.kid: Face your grown-up. Raise your thread hand. Look where the other thread is.

ask.q: Why are the threads on opposite sides now?
good: Because you turned round.
We are looking at each other.
Your right is on my left.

flow.parent: Facing each other, your right hand is across from your child's left hand. When you shake right hands, the arms cross.

rows.label: your hands, as you see them
your grown-up's, as you see them

chart.title: Face to face. Red is the thread hand.

flow.context: This is step 3 of Face to Face. You face your grown-up and see where the two thread hands are now.

flow.do: 1. Stay face to face. 2. Call out: touch my right hand with your left hand. 3. Then: touch my left knee. 4. Take turns to call. 5. Go slowly.
flow.say: Touch my right hand with your left hand. Look for my thread before you move.
flow.kid: Touch the hand your grown-up calls. Look for the thread first.

check.q: Your friend stands facing you. Where is her right hand?
check.why: She has turned to face you, so her right hand is across from your left hand. Picking 'across from my right hand' is true only when you both face the same way.

flow.context: This is the last step of Face to Face. You play a quick touching game to practise your grown-up's left and right.

activities.title: Maths in life: lay the leaf for a meal
activities.context: In this activity you set the banana leaf or the plate for a real meal at home. Every food has its place, and the places are said with position words. You also find out that the server and the eater see left and right the other way round.
activities.problem: Can you put each food in its place on the leaf, just by hearing where it goes?

materials.item: a banana leaf or a plate for each person at the meal
the cool foods of the meal: salt, pickle, a banana, appalam or chips
a tumbler of water for each person

activities.safety: A grown-up serves everything hot, such as rice, sambar and rasam. The child serves only the cool things.

schedule.what: Before a meal, lay each leaf or plate and put the cool foods in their places by position words.

activities.record: After the meal, draw the leaf from above. Draw each food in its place.

setup.art: A banana leaf on a floor mat with its narrow tip to the left of a seated child, and a tumbler of water beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the leaf. The narrow tip often goes on the eater's left.

setup.art: The leaf seen from above with a pinch of salt and a spoon of pickle at the top left, small heaps of vegetables along the top half, and the bottom half empty.
setup.caption: 2. Small foods on the top half. The bottom half waits for rice.

setup.art: A child standing across the leaf from a seated grandmother, reaching over to put a banana on the far left of the leaf as the grandmother sees it.
setup.caption: 3. You stand across from the eater. Her left is your right.

flow.do: 1. Sit where a person will eat. 2. Lay one leaf or plate in front of you. 3. On a leaf, find the narrow tip and the line down the middle. 4. Show the top half, far from you, and the bottom half, near you.
flow.say: Sit here like the person who will eat. Which half of the leaf is near you? Which half is far?
flow.kid: Sit where someone will eat. Find the top half and the bottom half of the leaf.
flow.parent: In many Tamil and Kerala homes the narrow tip is on the eater's left. Small foods go on the top half and rice on the bottom half. Families differ, so teach your own way.

rows.label: top half, far from the eater

chart.title: One way to lay a leaf: salt, pickle, vegetables, and rice below

flow.context: This is the first step of Lay the Leaf. You sit where a person will eat and find the top half and the bottom half of the leaf.

flow.do: 1. Stay seated on the eater's side. 2. Call each place aloud, one at a time. 3. Your child puts the cool food there. 4. Use your family's places.
flow.say: Put the salt at the top, on the left. Put the pickle next to the salt, on its right.
flow.kid: Listen for the place. Put each food there. Say the place aloud.

ask.q: Where did you put the banana? Say it in words.
good: At the top, on the left.
Next to the salt.
Above the rice place.

flow.context: This is step 2 of Lay the Leaf. You put the cool foods on one leaf, each in the place a grown-up calls out.

flow.do: 1. Now your child stands across the leaf, as a server does. 2. Ask where the eater's left is from here. 3. Your child lays the next leaf from the server's side. 4. Sit down and check it.
flow.say: Now stand across from me, like someone serving. The salt goes on my left. Which side is that for you?
flow.kid: Stand across from the eater. The salt goes on her left. Which side is that for you?

ask.q: From where you stand, is my left on your left or on your right?
good: On my right.
The other side.
Your left is my right.

flow.parent: This is the finding from Face to Face, used for real. If the salt lands on the wrong side, sit your child in the eater's place to look.

check.q: You stand facing a person who is eating. The salt goes on her left. Which side is that for you?
check.why: You face her, so her left is on your right. Picking 'my left' is correct only when you stand beside her and face the same way.

flow.context: This is step 3 of Lay the Leaf. You stand across the leaf like a server, and work out where the eater's left is.

flow.do: 1. Lay the other leaves or plates the same way. 2. Put a tumbler of water outside each leaf. 3. At the meal, ask each person to say where one food is.
flow.say: Every leaf should look the same to the person who sits at it. Check each one from their place.
flow.kid: Lay the other leaves the same way. Put a tumbler outside each leaf.
flow.context: This is the last step of Lay the Leaf. You lay the leaves for the whole family and check each one from the eater's place.

activities.title: Draw What I Say
activities.context: In this activity one person says where to draw each thing, and the other draws it without seeing any picture. It gives practice in hearing and using top, bottom, left, right, above and inside on a sheet of paper.
activities.problem: Can you make a picture from words alone? Can you tell someone a picture so well that theirs matches yours?

materials.item: plain paper
a pencil or crayons

schedule.what: Draw a picture from five spoken instructions. Then swap and give the instructions.

activities.record: Keep both drawings. Write the five instructions on the back of one.

setup.art: A child with a pencil and a blank sheet, and a grown-up beside her reading from a small slip of paper.
setup.caption: 1. One person speaks. One person draws.

setup.art: A child's drawing with a sun at the top in the middle, a pot at the bottom left with a fish inside, a tree on the right and a bird above the tree.
setup.caption: 2. Draw each thing where the words say.

setup.art: Two drawings side by side on a floor, the same picture drawn by two different hands, with a child pointing at one difference.
setup.caption: 3. Swap. Then compare the two pictures.

flow.do: 1. Give your child paper and a pencil. 2. Tie the thread on their right wrist if it helps. 3. Read the five instructions slowly, one at a time. 4. Wait for each drawing before the next.
flow.say: Draw a sun at the top, in the middle. Draw a pot at the bottom, on the left. Draw a tree on the right. Draw a bird above the tree. Draw a fish inside the pot.
flow.kid: Listen and draw. Put each thing where the words say.
flow.parent: Do not correct during the drawing. The picture in the chart shows roughly where each thing should end up.

chart.title: Sun, bird, tree and pot. A box with ? has nothing in it.

flow.context: This is the first step of Draw What I Say. A grown-up reads five instructions with position words, and you draw each thing in its place.

flow.do: 1. Look at the drawing together. 2. Read each instruction again. 3. Your child points to the thing and says where it is.
flow.say: Where is the bird? Tell me in words. What is below the bird?
flow.kid: Point to each thing. Say where it is on your paper.

ask.q: What is at the bottom, on the left?
good: The pot.
The pot with the fish inside.

flow.context: This is step 2 of Draw What I Say. You check your drawing by saying where each thing is.

flow.do: 1. Swap. Your child thinks of a picture with four things. 2. They tell you where to draw each one. 3. Draw exactly what they say. 4. Make one mistake on purpose for them to catch.
flow.say: Now you tell me what to draw, and where. I will draw only what your words say.
flow.kid: Now you say what to draw and where. Check your grown-up's picture for a mistake.

ask.q: What did I get wrong?
good: I said above, and you drew it below.
The ball should be on the right.
It should be inside the box.

check.q: You hear: 'Draw a bird above the tree.' Where does the bird go?
check.why: Above means higher than. Picking 'lower than the tree' mixes up above and below.

flow.context: This is the last step of Draw What I Say. Now you give the instructions, and you check the grown-up's drawing.

activities.title: The Step Count: near to what?
activities.context: In this activity you count your steps from the door to four things in a room, and put them in order from nearest to farthest. Then you count again from the window. It shows that near and far depend on where you start.
activities.problem: Which thing in the room is the nearest? Does the answer change if you stand somewhere else?

materials.item: four things in one room that stay put, such as a bed, a shelf, a chair and a window
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Count steps from the door to four things and order them. Then count from the window and compare.

activities.record: Make two lists: 'From the door' and 'From the window'. In each list write the four things with their steps, nearest first.

setup.art: A child standing in a doorway looking into a bedroom with a bed, a shelf, a chair and a window.
setup.caption: 1. Stand at the door. Guess which thing is nearest.

setup.art: The child walking heel to toe across the floor toward a shelf, counting on her fingers.
setup.caption: 2. Count your steps to each thing.

setup.art: The child now standing at the window, looking back at the same four things.
setup.caption: 3. Now start from the window. Count again.

flow.do: 1. Stand at the door with your child. 2. Pick four things in the room. 3. Ask which is nearest to the door and which is farthest. 4. Write the guesses.
flow.say: From the door, which of these four is the nearest? Which is the farthest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stand at the door. Which thing is nearest? Which is farthest? Guess.

chart.title: Steps from the door. Where will each thing be?

flow.context: This is the first step of the Step Count. You stand at the door and guess which of four things is nearest and which is farthest.

flow.do: 1. Your child walks from the door to each thing, with steps of the same size. 2. They count aloud. 3. Write the number of steps next to each thing. 4. Together, order the four from fewest steps to most.
flow.say: Walk to the shelf and count your steps. Keep your steps the same size each time.
flow.kid: Walk from the door to each thing. Count your steps. Write the number.

ask.q: Which thing took the fewest steps? So which is nearest?
good: The chair, 2 steps.
The one with the smallest number.

flow.parent: Heel-to-toe steps keep the size the same. Fewer steps means nearer.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the Step Count. You count your steps from the door to four things and order them from nearest to farthest.

flow.do: 1. Now stand at the window, or at the far wall. 2. Ask for a new guess: nearest and farthest from here. 3. Count the steps again. 4. Compare the two lists.
flow.say: Now we start from the window. Will the nearest thing be the same one? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Now stand at the window. Guess again. Then count your steps again.

ask.q: The bed was far before. Now the bed is near. Did the bed move?
good: No, I moved.
It is near the window and far from the door.
It depends where I stand.

check.q: The shop is 3 steps from the gate and 9 steps from the well. Is the shop near or far?
options: Near the gate, and farther from the well
check.why: Near and far need a starting place. 3 steps is near the gate. 9 steps is farther from the well. Picking only 'near' or only 'far' leaves out where you are counting from.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Step Count. You count your steps again from the window and find that the nearest thing has changed.

activities.title: Everyone does maths: dance like a honeybee
activities.context: In this activity you tell someone where a hidden sweet is, without any words, the way a honeybee tells her sisters where the flowers are. A long waggle means far. A short waggle means near.
activities.problem: Can you say 'near' or 'far', and which way, with a dance alone?

materials.item: a small sweet, a flower or a toy to hide
two rooms, or one room and a balcony

schedule.what: Hide a sweet near or far. Tell where it is with a waggle walk. Then swap.

activities.record: Draw a short wavy line and write 'near'. Draw a long wavy line and write 'far'.

setup.art: A child hiding a wrapped sweet behind a cushion while a grown-up waits in the next room with eyes closed.
setup.caption: 1. The bee hides the sweet, near or far.

setup.art: The child walking in a straight line toward a doorway, wiggling her hips, with a wavy line drawn along her path.
setup.caption: 2. Waggle toward it. Long waggle for far, short for near.

setup.art: The grown-up walking off in the direction the child pointed and finding the sweet.
setup.caption: 3. The other bee goes to look.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child how a honeybee tells her sisters where flowers are. 2. Show a short waggle walk of 2 steps and a long one of 8 steps. 3. Agree: the walk points straight at the hiding place.
flow.say: A honeybee has no words. She waggles. A long waggle means far. A short waggle means near.
flow.kid: A bee waggles to tell where flowers are. Long waggle: far. Short waggle: near.
flow.parent: This is simpler than the real dance. A real bee dances on the wall of the comb, in the dark. Her angle from straight up shows the angle from the Sun.

chart.title: The bee code for this game

flow.context: This is the first step of Dance Like a Honeybee. You learn the code: a long waggle walk means far, and a short one means near.

flow.do: 1. Close your eyes. Your child hides the sweet near or far. 2. They come back to the middle of the room. 3. They waggle toward the hiding place, long or short. 4. You go and look.
flow.say: No words, little bee. Dance for me. I will fly where your dance tells me.
flow.kid: Hide the sweet. Come back. Waggle toward it. Use no words.

ask.q: After I find it: how did your dance tell me it was far?
good: I waggled for a long time.
I took many steps.

flow.context: This is step 2 of Dance Like a Honeybee. You hide a sweet and tell a grown-up where it is with a waggle walk and no words.

flow.do: 1. Swap. You hide the sweet and dance. 2. Your child reads your dance and finds it. 3. Ask what the dance told them and what it did not.
flow.say: Now I am the bee. Watch my waggle. Is it near or far? Which way?
flow.kid: Watch your grown-up waggle. Near or far? Which way? Go and look.

ask.q: What did my dance leave out?
good: If it was under or inside something.
How high it was.
Exactly where.

check.q: A honeybee makes a very long waggle run. What is she telling her sisters?
check.why: A longer waggle run means the flowers are farther from the hive. A short run means they are near.

flow.context: This is the last step of Dance Like a Honeybee. You read a grown-up's waggle walk to find the sweet.

games.title: Three in a Line
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a dice game played on a shelf of nine boxes: three rows with three places in each. Two rolls tell you a row and a place. You say the place aloud and put a bean there. It builds quick use of top, middle, bottom, left and right.

printables.title: A shelf for each player: draw 9 boxes in 3 rows, with these names
The dice key
items: First roll gives the row. 1 or 2 = top. 3 or 4 = middle. 5 or 6 = bottom.
Second roll gives the place. 1 or 2 = left. 3 or 4 = middle. 5 or 6 = right.

rules: Each player draws a shelf of 9 boxes, 3 rows of 3, and takes 9 beans.
On your turn, roll the dice twice. The first roll gives the row. The second roll gives the place in that row.
Say the box aloud, such as 'bottom row, on the left'. Then put a bean in that box on your own shelf.
If that box already has a bean, say the box aloud anyway. Your turn ends.
If you say the wrong box, another player may correct you. Then you put the bean in the correct box.
The first player with three beans in a line wins. The line can go across, down, or from corner to corner.
Playing alone: count how many turns you need to make a line. Play again and compare.

setup.art: Two sheets of paper on a floor, each with a hand-drawn grid of nine boxes, a dice between them and two small heaps of beans.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your shelf: 3 rows, 3 boxes in each.

setup.art: A dice showing 5 and then 2, and a child's hand putting a bean in the bottom left box of her grid.
setup.caption: 2. Roll twice. Say the box. Put a bean there.

setup.art: A grid with three beans in a line from the top left corner to the bottom right corner, and a child cheering.
setup.caption: 3. Three in a line wins.

flow.do: 1. Each player draws 9 boxes, in 3 rows of 3. 2. Point to the top, middle and bottom rows. 3. Point to the left, middle and right box in a row. 4. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: This is your shelf. Show me the top row. Show me the box on the right of the bottom row.
flow.kid: Draw 9 boxes, 3 in each row. Find the top row. Find the left side.

chart.title: Your shelf: left, middle, right in each row

flow.context: This is the first step of Three in a Line, a dice game on a shelf of nine boxes. Here you draw your shelf and find its rows and sides.

flow.do: 1. Show the dice key. 2. Play one practice turn each. 3. Say the box aloud before the bean goes down.
flow.say: I rolled 5, then 2. Five means the bottom row. Two means the left. So I say: bottom row, on the left.
flow.kid: Roll twice. The first roll is the row. The second is the place. Say the box aloud.

check.q: You roll 1, then 6. Where does your bean go?
check.why: The first roll, 1, means the top row. The second roll, 6, means the right. Picking 'bottom row, on the left' swaps the two rolls.

flow.context: This is step 2 of Three in a Line, a dice game on a shelf of nine boxes. Here you learn the dice key and play a practice turn.

flow.do: 1. Play the game, taking turns. 2. Now and then, ask a player which box they still need for a line. 3. Ask them to name it with position words.
flow.say: Which box do you need now to make a line? Tell me its row and its place.
flow.kid: Play in turns. Say each box aloud. Try to get three in a line.

ask.q: You have top left and bottom right. Which box would finish that line?
good: The middle one.
Middle row, in the middle.

flow.context: This is step 3 of Three in a Line, a dice game on a shelf of nine boxes. Here you play, and name the boxes you still need.

flow.do: 1. When someone has three in a line, the game ends. 2. The winner says where the three beans are. 3. Count the empty boxes on each shelf.
flow.say: Tell us your three boxes. How many of your boxes are still empty?
flow.kid: Three in a line wins. Say where your three beans are.
flow.context: This is the last step of Three in a Line, a dice game on a shelf of nine boxes. Here the winner names the three boxes of the line.

games.title: Amma Says
games.players: 1 or more players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is an action game played with 16 cards. Each card gives an order with position words, such as 'left hand above your head'. You do it only when the caller first says 'Amma says'. It builds quick left and right, and in front, behind, inside and outside.

printables.title: 16 action cards to cut out, or to copy on slips of paper
items: Left hand on your left knee
Right hand on your left ear
Left hand on your right shoulder
Left hand below your right hand
Stand in front of the chair
Stand between the chair and the ring
Put one foot inside the ring

rules: Tie a thread on every player's right wrist. Put a chair in the middle. Lay a ring of thread or a dupatta on the floor.
Each player starts with 5 beans. Shuffle the 16 cards. One person is the caller.
The caller takes a card and reads it. Sometimes the caller says 'Amma says' first, and sometimes not.
If the caller said 'Amma says', do the action at once. If not, stay still.
If you use the wrong side, go to the wrong place, or move when you should stay still, give up one bean.
The game ends when all 16 cards are used. The player with the most beans wins.
Playing alone: turn over a card, do the action, then check with your thread. Count how many of the 16 you got correct.

setup.art: Three children with red threads on their right wrists standing round a chair, with a ring made from a dupatta on the floor nearby.
setup.caption: 1. Thread on each right wrist. A chair and a ring on the floor.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a small card and calling out, while the children each put a left hand above their heads.
setup.caption: 2. The caller reads a card. Do it only after 'Amma says'.

setup.art: One child holding up the wrong hand and laughing as she drops a bean into a bowl.
setup.caption: 3. Wrong side? Give up a bean. Most beans wins.

flow.do: 1. Tie a thread on each right wrist. 2. Put the chair in the middle and the ring on the floor. 3. Give each player 5 beans. 4. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: Show me your right hand. Show me your left foot. Now stand inside the ring. Now outside.
flow.kid: Tie the thread on your right wrist. Show your right hand. Show your left foot.
flow.context: This is the first step of Amma Says, an action game with 16 cards of position words. Here you set up the chair, the ring and the threads.

flow.do: 1. Play three practice cards with no beans lost. 2. For one of them, leave out 'Amma says'. 3. Show that everyone must stay still for that one.
flow.say: Amma says: right hand on your left ear. Good. Now: hop on your left foot. Did I say 'Amma says'?
flow.kid: Do the action only after 'Amma says'. If you hear no 'Amma says', stay still.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Amma Says, an action game with 16 cards of position words. Here you practise with three cards before the game begins.

flow.do: 1. Play through the 16 cards. 2. Call slowly at first, then faster. 3. Let your child be the caller for the last few cards.
flow.say: Amma says: stand between the chair and the ring. Amma says: left hand on your right shoulder.
flow.kid: Listen for 'Amma says'. Then do it fast. Use the correct side.
flow.parent: Cards that cross the body, such as 'right hand on your left ear', are the hardest. Slow down for those.

check.q: Amma says: stand behind the chair. Where do you go?
options: To the side of the chair's back rest
To the side where you sit down
check.why: A chair has a front of its own, the side you face when you sit on it. Behind the chair is the side of its back rest. That stays the same wherever the caller stands.

flow.context: This is step 3 of Amma Says, an action game with 16 cards of position words. Here you play through the cards and lose a bean for each slip.

flow.do: 1. When the cards are finished, count each player's beans. 2. Ask which card was the hardest and why.
flow.say: Count your beans. Which card tricked you the most? Why was that one hard?
flow.kid: Count your beans. Most beans wins. Which card was the hardest?
flow.context: This is the last step of Amma Says, an action game with 16 cards of position words. Here you count the beans and say which card was hardest.

projects.title: Everyone does maths: ask a seed which way is down
projects.context: In this five-day project you sprout moong seeds against the wall of a glass tumbler, so that you can see the roots. Then you turn the tumbler on its side. You find out whether a root knows which way is down.
projects.problem: A seed has no eyes and sits in the dark. If we turn the seed, will the root still find the way down?

materials.item: whole green moong, or chana
a clear glass tumbler, or a clear plastic jar
tissue paper, cotton or a piece of old cotton cloth
water, and a plate to rest the tumbler on

projects.safety: Keep beans, seeds and other small things away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them. Do not eat these seeds after the test.

schedule.what: Soak 8 moong seeds in water overnight.
Line the tumbler with wet tissue. Tuck the seeds between the tissue and the glass.
Look for the white roots. Draw which way they point.
Guess what the roots will do. Then lay the tumbler on its side.
Look at the root tips. Draw which way they point now.

projects.record: Each day from day 3, draw the tumbler and one seed with the root. Add an arrow to show which way the root tip points.

setup.art: A glass tumbler lined with wet tissue paper, with six green moong seeds held between the tissue and the glass, halfway up.
setup.caption: 1. Tuck soaked seeds between wet tissue and the glass.

setup.art: The same tumbler two days later, each seed with a short white root pointing down.
setup.caption: 2. Wait for the roots. Which way do they grow?

setup.art: The tumbler lying on its side on a plate, and a close view of a root whose tip has bent to point down again.
setup.caption: 3. Lay the tumbler on its side. Look again the next day.

flow.do: 1. Count 8 moong seeds into a cup. 2. Cover them with water. 3. Leave them overnight.
flow.say: These seeds are alive and resting. Water will wake them. Where do you think the root will come out?
flow.kid: Count 8 seeds into a cup. Cover them with water. Leave them for the night.
flow.wait: Leave the seeds in water overnight.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Ask a Seed, a five-day project with sprouting moong. On day 1 you soak 8 moong seeds in water.

flow.do: 1. Line the inside of the tumbler with wet tissue. 2. Tuck 6 soaked seeds between the tissue and the glass, halfway up. 3. Turn the seeds different ways. 4. Keep the tissue wet every day.
flow.say: Put each seed where we can see them through the glass. Turn some sideways and some upside down.
flow.kid: Tuck the seeds between the wet tissue and the glass. Turn them different ways.
flow.parent: Two seeds are spare. Keep the tumbler out of strong sun and add a spoon of water when the tissue dries.
flow.context: This is day 2 of Ask a Seed, a five-day project with sprouting moong. On day 2 you tuck the soaked seeds between wet tissue and the glass of a tumbler.

flow.do: 1. Look at the seeds through the glass. 2. Find the white roots. 3. Ask which way each root points. 4. Your child draws one seed with an arrow.
flow.say: The seeds were turned in different ways. Which way did each root go? What do you notice?
flow.kid: Find the white roots. Which way does each one point? Draw one.

ask.q: The seeds faced different ways. Did the roots go different ways?
good: No, all of them go down.
Some started sideways and then went down.

flow.parent: If no root shows yet, wait one more day. In cool weather sprouting is slower.
flow.context: This is day 3 of Ask a Seed, a five-day project with sprouting moong. On day 3 you look at which way the new roots are growing.

flow.do: 1. Ask what the roots will do if the tumbler lies on its side. 2. Ask for a reason. 3. Lay the tumbler on its side on a plate. 4. Do not turn it again.
flow.say: Now the roots will point sideways. What will they do by tomorrow? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess what the roots will do. Then lay the tumbler on its side.

ask.q: What is your guess, and why?
good: They will keep going sideways, because that is how they are now.
They will turn down, because roots go down.
I do not know.

flow.wait: Leave the tumbler on its side until tomorrow.
flow.context: This is day 4 of Ask a Seed, a five-day project with sprouting moong. On day 4 you guess what the roots will do, and then lay the tumbler on its side.

flow.do: 1. Look closely at the tip of each root. 2. Your child draws one root with an arrow at the tip. 3. Ask what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Look at the tips. Which way do they point now? What do you think the root can sense?
flow.kid: Look at the root tips. Which way do they point now? Draw one.

ask.q: What did you find out about roots?
good: The tips turned down again.
The root knows which way is down.
Even lying sideways, the seed finds down.

flow.parent: The tips usually bend down within a day. If the bend is small, leave the tumbler one more day. A root senses the pull of the Earth and grows toward it.

check.q: A sprouting seed is laid sideways. Which way does the tip of the root grow next?
check.why: A root senses which way is down and bends to grow that way. Picking 'sideways' means the root was expected to keep the way it first had.

flow.context: This is day 5 of Ask a Seed, a five-day project with sprouting moong. On day 5 you look at the root tips after a day on their side.

challenges.title: Stretch: back to back, build the same thing
challenges.context: This is a design challenge that goes past Class 1. Two people sit back to back with the same five things. One builds something and tells the other how to build it too, with words alone. You invent a way of telling that does not go wrong.
challenges.problem: Your partner cannot see what you built. Tell them so clearly that their five things end up in exactly the same places as yours.
constraints: You sit back to back. Nobody may turn round or peek until the end.
Words only. No pointing, and no touching the other person's things.
The builder may say each instruction twice. The listener may ask questions.
materials: two sets of the same five things: a plate, a tumbler, a spoon, a lemon and a matchbox
two sheets of newspaper to build on
a thread for each right wrist
general: Say each thing and where it goes compared with the plate: 'the tumbler is on the plate'.
Use left and right: 'the spoon is on the left of the plate'.
Go slowly, one thing at a time, and ask the listener to say it back.
creative: Before you start, agree on something both of you can find, such as the window. Then say 'the spoon is on the window side of the plate'.
Name the four sides of the newspaper first: the side near you, the far side, the window side and the door side.
Fold each newspaper into four boxes and number them 1 to 4, in the same way. Then say which box each thing goes in.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way of telling. Test it with a new build. If the two builds do not match, find the word that went wrong and change your way.

setup.art: A girl and her mother sitting back to back on the floor, each with a sheet of newspaper and the same five things: a plate, a tumbler, a spoon, a lemon and a matchbox.
setup.caption: 1. Sit back to back. Each has the same five things.

setup.art: The girl's build: a tumbler on a plate, a spoon to one side, a lemon inside the tumbler and a matchbox in front, while she speaks over her shoulder.
setup.caption: 2. One builds and tells. The other listens and builds.

setup.art: The two turned round, looking at both builds side by side, the girl pointing at a spoon that is on the wrong side.
setup.caption: 3. Turn round. Do the two builds match?

flow.do: 1. Sit back to back, each with a newspaper and the five things. 2. Your child builds something with all five. 3. They tell you how to build it. 4. Do exactly what the words say. 5. Turn round and compare.
flow.say: Build something with your five things. Then tell me how to build the same. I cannot see yours.
flow.kid: Build with your five things. Tell your grown-up how to build the same.
flow.parent: Follow the words exactly, even when you can guess what was meant. If your child says 'on the left', use your own left. The first builds often do not match.

chart.title: Each builder has the same things

flow.context: This is the first step of the back-to-back challenge, where one person tells another what to build. Here you try it once and see whether the two builds match.

flow.do: 1. Look at both builds. 2. Find each thing that is in a different place. 3. Ask which word caused it. 4. Read the usual ways and the creative ways aloud if your child wants ideas.
flow.say: Which things are not in the same place? Which word went wrong? How could we say it better?
flow.kid: Find what does not match. Which word went wrong? Think of a better way to say it.

ask.q: You said 'left'. We sit back to back. Is your left the same side as my left?
good: No. We face different ways.
Your left is toward the door and mine is toward the window.

flow.context: This is step 2 of the back-to-back challenge, where one person tells another what to build. Here you find which words went wrong and think of a better way to tell.

flow.do: 1. Agree on your child's new way of telling. 2. Sit back to back again. 3. This time you build and tell, using their way. 4. Compare. 5. Then swap once more.
flow.say: We will use your new way. This time I build and you listen. Then we look.
flow.kid: Use your new way. Your grown-up builds and tells. You build the same.

check.q: Two people sit back to back. Which clue means the same side for both of them?
check.why: The window stays where it is for both people. Back to back, one person's left is toward a different wall from the other person's left.

flow.context: This is step 3 of the back-to-back challenge, where one person tells another what to build. Here you test your new way of telling with a fresh build.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to explain their way to someone else at home. 2. Ask if it would work over the phone, with a cousin in another town.
flow.say: Would your way work on the phone, with someone in another house? What would you have to change?
flow.kid: Tell someone how your way works. Would it work over the phone?

ask.q: Your cousin's house has no window on that side. What could you both use?
good: The side near you and the far side.
Numbers on the paper.
North and south, if we both know them.

flow.context: This is the last step of the back-to-back challenge, where one person tells another what to build. Here you explain your way and ask if it would work over the phone.

items.p: Which shape is on the top shelf, on the left?
items.why: Top tells you the shelf. Left tells you the end. The blue square is there. The yellow circle is on the left too, but on the bottom shelf.

items.p: Look at the row. The shape between the circle and the triangle is a ____.
items.why: The square has the circle on one side and the triangle on the other. That is what between means.

items.p: In the picture, the red circle is above the blue square.
items.why: True. The red circle is on the higher shelf, so it is above the blue square.

items.p: A lemon is in a closed tiffin box. Where is the lemon?
items.why: The lemon is within the walls and the lid, so the lemon is inside. To get out, the lemon would have to cross the edge.

items.p: You stand at your front door. Sort each thing: near or far?
items.why: You can touch the doormat, the chappals and the handle from the door. The Moon, the Sun and the stars are a very long way off.

items.p: Match each position word to its opposite.
items.why: Each pair names two opposite places: the highest and the lowest, within and not within, a short way and a long way, the two sides, higher and lower.

items.p: Which shape is at the right end of the row?
items.why: The red rectangle is the last shape on the right. The green triangle is at the left end.

items.p: Count the shapes on the bottom shelf. There are ____ shapes.
items.why: Bottom means the lowest shelf. Touch each shape there once: 1, 2, 3, 4.

items.p: A cup is on a table. You walk round the table. The cup is still on the table.
items.why: True. 'On' is about the cup and the table only. You moved, but they did not.

items.p: Draw a table. Draw a ball under the table and a cup on the table.
items.a: A table with a cup resting on its top and a ball on the floor below it.
items.why: A strong drawing has the cup touching the top of the table, and the ball lower than the table top, between its legs.

items.p: Draw a box. Draw 3 dots inside the box and 2 dots outside the box.
items.a: A closed box shape with 3 dots within its lines and 2 dots beyond them.
items.why: To check, ask of each dot: would it have to cross a line to get out? The 3 inside dots would. The 2 outside dots would not.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. Look around you. What is above your head? What is below your feet?
items.a: For example: the fan is above my head, and the floor is below my feet.
items.why: A strong answer names a real thing that is higher than the head, and a real thing that is lower than the feet.

items.p: Which shape is second from the left?
items.why: Start at the left end and count: the green triangle is first, the red circle is second. The yellow circle is second from the right.

items.p: How many shapes are on the right of the blue square? ____
items.why: After the blue square, going right, come the yellow circle and the red rectangle. That is 2 shapes.

items.p: You and a friend face each other. Your right hand is across from your friend's right hand.
items.why: False. Your friend has turned to face you, so your right hand is across from your friend's left hand.

items.p: Put these in order, from nearest the door to farthest from the door.
items.why: Fewer steps means nearer. 1 is the fewest, then 4, then 7, then 10.

items.p: Lakshmi is in a queue. 2 children are in front of her and 2 are behind. How many children in all?
items.why: 2 in front, 2 behind, and Lakshmi herself: 2 and 1 and 2 make 5. Picking 4 leaves Lakshmi out.

items.p: You walk to the other side of a table. Sort each word: stays true, or can change?
items.why: On, under and inside are about the things only. Left and right are about you too, so they swap when you face the other way.

items.p: Look at the shelf. The green triangle is in the ____ row.
items.why: The green triangle has one row above and one row below. That row is the middle row.

items.p: On roads in India, which side do vehicles keep to?
items.why: In India everyone keeps to the left. People agreed on one side so that vehicles do not meet head on. Many other countries chose the right.

items.p: Draw a row of three shapes: a triangle on the left, a circle on the right, a square between them.
items.a: Triangle, square, circle, from left to right.
items.why: A strong drawing has the square in the middle, with the triangle at the left end and the circle at the right end.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. The book went from your left to your right. Why?
items.a: Because I walked to the other side and faced the other way. The book did not move.
items.why: A strong answer says that the child moved, not the book. Left and right go with the person.

items.p: A tumbler and a plate sit on a mat. Two children face each other across the mat.

views.says: The tumbler is on the left of the plate. I can see it.
No. The tumbler is on the right of the plate.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? What could they both say that is true for the two of them?
items.a: A strong answer says that each child is correct from her own side, and offers a clue that works for both, such as 'the tumbler is on the window side'.
items.why: The children face opposite ways, so one child's left is the other child's right. A clue that uses a fixed thing, such as the window, is the same for both.

items.p: Draw round both your hands on paper. Colour the right hand red.
items.a: Two hand outlines. The outline of the right hand is red.
items.why: To check, put your hands back on the outlines. The red outline should be under the hand with the thread, your right hand.

items.p: Which shape is below the red circle and on the left of the blue square?
items.why: Below the red circle are the green triangle and the yellow rectangle. On the left of the blue square are the green triangle and the blue circle. Only the green triangle fits both clues.

items.p: Six children stand in a row. Nila is 3rd from the left. From the right she is number ____.
items.why: This one goes past Class 1. Count from the right end: 1, 2, 3, and Nila is the 4th. Three children are on her right and two are on her left.

items.p: Down points the same way for a child in Chennai and a child on the far side of the Earth.
items.why: False. Down is toward the middle of the Earth. The two children stand on opposite sides of a ball, so their 'down' arrows point toward each other.

items.p: You face a mirror and raise your right hand. Where is the raised hand in the mirror?
opts: On the same side as my right hand
On the side of my left hand
items.why: In a mirror, the raised hand is straight across from your raised hand, on the same side. A friend facing you is different: her right hand is across from your left.

items.p: The pot is below the plate. The lid is above the plate. Put them in order, top first.
items.why: The lid is above the plate, so the lid is at the top. The pot is below the plate, so the pot is at the bottom.

items.p: Match each thing to the place where you find it.
pairs: at the top of a house
on the outside of a banana
items.why: A roof covers the top. Roots grow down into the soil. The yolk is within the shell. The peel is the outer cover.

items.p: Count the shapes that are NOT in the middle row. There are ____ shapes.
items.why: The top row has 3 shapes and the bottom row has 3 shapes. 3 and 3 make 6.

items.p: Sort each one: above the ground or below the ground?
items.why: A kite, a cloud and a nest are higher than the ground. A carrot, well water and a worm's tunnel are lower than the ground.

items.p: Which shape is in the bottom right corner?
items.why: Bottom tells you the lowest row. Right tells you the end. The green circle is there. The red square is at the bottom left, and the green square is at the top right.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. Tell where your toothbrush is, without pointing. Use two position words.
items.a: For example: my toothbrush is inside the blue mug, on the shelf above the tap.
items.why: A strong answer uses two position words and names the other things, so that a visitor could find the toothbrush.

items.p: Draw 9 boxes, in 3 rows of 3. Draw a star in the top right box.
items.a: A 3 by 3 grid with a star in the last box of the first row.
items.why: Top chooses the row. Right chooses the place in that row.

items.p: Is the Moon near or far?

views.says: Far. A rocket took about three days to carry people there.
Near. The Sun is about 400 times farther away than the Moon.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other child has correct.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, and sees that near and far depend on what you compare with.
items.why: Next to a trip to the shop, the Moon is very far. Next to the Sun, the Moon is near. Near and far always need something to compare with.

quiz.p: Which shape is on the bottom shelf, in the middle?
quiz.why: Bottom tells you the shelf. Middle tells you the place. The red triangle is there. The red circle is in the middle too, but on the top shelf.

quiz.p: A lemon is under a stool. You walk to the other side of the stool. The lemon is still under the stool.
quiz.why: True. 'Under' is about the lemon and the stool. Neither of them moved.

quiz.p: A coin is in your closed fist. Where is the coin?
quiz.why: Your fingers close round the coin like walls. The coin is inside your hand.

quiz.p: The well is 3 steps from the door. The gate is 8 steps from the door. Which is nearer the door?
quiz.why: Fewer steps means nearer. 3 is fewer than 8, so the well is nearer the door.

quiz.p: A thread is on your right hand. You turn around. Which hand has the thread now?
quiz.why: Your right hand is always your right hand. It turns with you. Only the things around you change sides.

quiz.p: How many shapes are on the left of the square? ____
quiz.why: Going left from the square you meet 3 shapes: a circle, a triangle and another circle.

quiz.p: Which shape is between the two circles?
quiz.why: The triangle has a circle on each side. The square and the rectangle are at the two ends.

quiz.p: Meena is first in the bus queue. Where are all the other people?
quiz.why: The first person has nobody in front. Everyone else in the queue stands behind her.

quiz.p: Put the spoon inside the tumbler, and the tumbler on the plate. What is at the bottom?
quiz.why: The tumbler rests on the plate, so the plate is lowest. The spoon is inside the tumbler, above the plate.

quiz.p: 'Put a bean in the top row, on the right.' Which shape does your bean cover?
quiz.why: The top row is the highest row. Its right end is the green square. The green circle is on the right too, but in the bottom row.

quiz.p: Which word can stop being true when you walk to the other side of a table?
quiz.why: 'On my left' has you in it. When you face the other way, the thing is on your right. On and under are about the things only.

quiz.p: Two friends face each other. A book on one friend's left is on the other friend's right.
quiz.why: True. They face opposite ways, so one friend's left side is the other friend's right side.

applications: A postal address says where a house is: the door number, the street, the town.
A bus conductor tells you where to get down: 'the stop after the temple'.
A cook follows position words: 'put the lid on the pot', 'keep the curd inside the fridge'.
A cricket captain sets the field by telling each fielder where to stand: near the bat, or far out by the rope.
A dance teacher calls 'right foot in front, left hand above your head', and the whole class moves together.
A doctor asks 'where does it hurt?' and you answer with position words: 'below my knee, on the left'.
A tailor sews the pocket on the left side of a shirt, above the waist.
Drivers keep to the left on Indian roads, so that vehicles going opposite ways do not meet.

open_questions.q: Is space a real thing by itself, or only a way of saying how things sit beside each other?
open_questions.why_open: Newton said space is real by itself. Leibniz, who lived at the same time, said it is only the order of things. Scientists and thinkers still argue.

open_questions.q: How do birds who fly across the world know which way to go?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that many birds use the Sun, the stars and the Earth's magnetism. How a bird's body senses that magnetism is still not settled.

open_questions.q: Does the universe have a middle or an edge?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody has found a middle or an edge. Nobody knows if space goes on for ever.

open_questions.q: Do people who speak with north and south think about places differently from people who speak with left and right?
open_questions.why_open: Some tests suggest they do, and other scientists read the same tests differently. The argument is still going on.

jokes.a: Neither. It is better to write with a pencil!

jokes.j: What did the left eye say to the right eye?
jokes.a: Between you and me, something smells.

maths.problem: Look at the shelf. Go to the row below the top row. How many shapes are in that row?
maths.answer: It is the middle row, and 3 shapes are in that row.
maths.explain: The row below the top row is the middle row. Count the shapes there: 1, 2, 3.
maths.context: In Three in a Line you found boxes by their row: top, middle or bottom. This uses the rows of a shelf to choose what to count.
maths.why_maths: A position word tells you which things to count, so you count the correct group.

maths.problem: From the door, the bed is 6 steps away and the shelf is 9 steps away. Which is nearer the door? How many steps nearer?
maths.answer: The bed is nearer, by 3 steps.
maths.explain: 6 is fewer than 9, so the bed is nearer. From 6, count on to 9: 7, 8, 9. That is 3 steps.
maths.context: In the Step Count you counted your steps from the door to things in the room. This compares two of those counts.
maths.why_maths: Counting steps turns 'near' and 'far' into numbers, and numbers can be compared exactly.

maths.problem: Five children stand in a row. Meena is in the middle. How many children are on her left? How many are on her right?
maths.answer: 2 on her left and 2 on her right.
maths.explain: Take Meena out of the 5, and 4 are left. The middle has the same number on each side. 2 and 2 make 4.
maths.context: In Amma Says you stood between two things. This asks how many are on each side of the one in the middle.
maths.why_maths: The middle of a row is the place with the same number on both sides. Counting each side lets you check.

maths.problem: Kavya and Farhan face each other across a mat. Kavya sees the plate on the left and the tumbler on the right. What does Farhan see on his left?
maths.answer: Farhan sees the tumbler on his left.
maths.explain: Farhan faces the other way. So Kavya's right is Farhan's left. The tumbler is on Kavya's right, so it is on Farhan's left.
maths.context: In Face to Face you found that your right hand is across from the other person's left hand. This uses that finding at a meal.
maths.why_maths: Knowing that left and right swap for a person who faces you lets you work out what they see without walking round.

roots.context: We said where things are: on, under, inside, near, left and right. Now let us ask what a place really is.

deep_truth.truth: In the Turn-Around Test, the book was on your left. You walked to the other side, and the same book was on your right. The book did not move. So left and right are not in the book. They are in the one who looks.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'the book is on the left' as if the left were a part of the room. But a room has no left side until someone stands in it and faces one way.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Turn-Around Test, 'on', 'under' and 'inside' stayed true wherever you stood. 'Left', 'right' and 'near' changed as soon as you moved.

three.who_am_i: You are the middle of your own left and right, your own front and back. Wherever you go, they go with you.
three.what_is_life: Every living being knows where things are. A bee dances to tell her sisters how far the flowers are. A root grows down, even in the dark.
three.what_is_this_world: A room has no left side and no near side by itself. It gets them when someone stands in it and looks.

roots.thread: Where is the lemon? You cannot say it with the lemon alone. You need a second thing: under the stool. Every position word joins one thing to another thing, or to you. So nothing has a place all by itself, only a place among the other things.

teachings.teaching: The Isha Upanishad speaks of the One that is in everything. It says: it moves, and it does not move. It is far, and it is near. It is inside all this, and it is outside all this.
teachings.link: Far and near sound like opposites. But in the Step Count the same bed was far from the door and near to the window. Both words were true of one bed.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha told of men who had been blind from birth. Each was led to a different part of one elephant. The man at the head said an elephant is like a water pot. The man at the ear said an elephant is like a winnowing basket. They began to fight.
teachings.link: Where each man stood decided what he found. In the Turn-Around Test, where you stood decided what was on your left. Each view was true from its own place.

science.text: Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, a language of Australia, mostly do not use left and right to say where things are. They use words like north, south, east and west (John Haviland, 1998, and Stephen Levinson, 1997). So people can live well without the words left and right.
Is space a real thing by itself, or only our way of saying how things sit beside each other? Scientists and thinkers still argue about this.

other_view.who: Isaac Newton, an English scientist, in his book of 1687
other_view.view: Newton said that space is real by itself. It is like one huge, still room that holds everything. Each thing has its own true place in that room, even if nobody is looking and nothing else is near. On this view, 'left' and 'near' are only our words. The book's place is a fact, with or without us.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out what 'down' means? This card tells the true story of an old mistake about the round Earth.
how_we_found_out.story: Long ago, many people thought that down was one direction for the whole world, like the floor of one giant room. So if the Earth were a ball, the people on the far side would hang upside down and fall off. About 1,700 years ago a Roman writer named Lactantius laughed at the round Earth for this reason. He asked who could believe in people whose feet are higher than their heads. In India, the mathematician Aryabhata saw it another way. In his book of 499 CE he compared the Earth to the round head of a kadamba flower, which is covered with tiny blossoms on every side. In the same way, he wrote, the round Earth is covered on every side by the living beings of land and water. Later, sailors settled it. In 1522 the ship Victoria came home to Spain after sailing right round the world. Nobody on the far side had fallen off. Down is not one direction. Down is toward the middle of the Earth, wherever you stand.
how_we_found_out.who: Aryabhata, and the sailors of the ship Victoria
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Down is the same direction everywhere, so people on the far side of a round Earth would fall off. Voyages round the world showed this was wrong. People live on every side of the Earth, and each stands with feet toward the middle.

Root gravitropism: gravity is sensed in the root cap, where starch-filled grains settle to the lower side of certain cells (the starch-statolith model, the leading explanation), and the root bends in the growing zone behind the tip.

Lactantius, Divine Institutes, Book 3, chapter 24 (early 4th century CE): mocks the idea of people whose feet are higher than their heads.
The ship Victoria, under Juan Sebastián Elcano, returned to Spain in September 1522 after the first voyage round the world, begun under Ferdinand Magellan in 1519.
Newton, I. (1687). Principia, Scholium to the Definitions: absolute space. The Leibniz-Clarke letters (1715-1716) give the opposing view that space is the order of things.

Left-hand traffic: about 70 to 76 countries and territories, with roughly a third of the world's people, keep left (counts differ by source). India, Sri Lanka and Japan keep left. France and the United States keep right.

Banana leaf meals: Onmanorama food features (Kerala sadya) place the narrow tip on the eater's left, small dishes on the upper half and rice on the lower half. Tamil practice is described similarly, but families and regions differ.

playtest: Walked through every flow as a family of two in a flat. The Turn-Around Test needs a stool, a tumbler, a spoon, a lemon, a book and a plate. From the other side, left and right swap and the rest stay. From far away, only 'near' changes. In a very small room, walk into the next room for the far step. Three in a Line was played in the head: a line usually comes in 6 to 10 turns, and a player alone can count turns. Amma Says uses all 16 cards once, and a child alone can check each card with the thread. Step minutes add up to each activity's minutes. Ask a Seed: moong soaked overnight usually shows a root within a day or two, and a root laid sideways usually bends down within a day, but this timing was not checked against a written source and is slower in cool weather. Facts looked up on the web while writing: Isha Upanishad 5, the Tittha Sutta (Udana 6.4), the Guugu Yimithirr direction words, the honeybee waggle dance and the 1973 Nobel Prize, the three mountains test and the Hughes test of 1975, Lactantius on people with feet above their heads, Aryabhata's kadamba flower verse, countries that keep left, and how a root senses down. Three things to know. The Aryabhata verse is numbered Gola 7 in some editions and 6 to 7 in others, and its wording here is a paraphrase. The banana leaf layout was confirmed for the Kerala sadya, and Tamil homes vary, so the activity tells families to use their own way. The return of the ship Victoria in 1522, Newton's book of 1687 and the three-day trip to the Moon were written from general knowledge and not looked up again. The three videos were confirmed by title and channel only, not watched, so watch each one before showing it.
